body_text:
The Density of Rationals and Irrationals. Between any two distinct
real numbers $x < y$, there exists both a rational number
$q \in \mathbb{Q}$ and an irrational number
$r \in \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}$ satisfying:
$$ x < q < y \quad \text{and} \quad x < r < y. $$

*Proof Sketch*:
1. **Rationals**: Since $y - x > 0$, by the Archimedean property
   there exists $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $n(y - x) > 1$, so
   $ny - nx > 1$. Let $m = \lfloor nx \rfloor + 1 \in \mathbb{Z}$.
   Then $nx < m \leq nx + 1 < ny$. Dividing by $n > 0$ yields
   $x < m/n < y$. Setting $q = m/n \in \mathbb{Q}$ proves density
   of $\mathbb{Q}$.
2. **Irrationals**: Since $x < y$, consider
   $x/\sqrt{2} < y/\sqrt{2}$. By density of rationals, choose a
   nonzero rational $q' \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
   $x/\sqrt{2} < q' < y/\sqrt{2}$. Then $r = q'\sqrt{2}$ is
   irrational and satisfies $x < r < y$.

Thus every open interval $(x, y) \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ contains
infinitely many rational and infinitely many irrational numbers.
